Sara Sheftel

Sara Sheftel

Sara Sheftel  

We live in a chaotic, aggressive world, marked by destruction. This destruction is rife in private and public life; it transcends national boundaries and permeates all sectors of society. The 20th century could well be known as the age of destructive impulsivity.

As analysts, we are interested in understanding how aggressive impulses take hold of the personality, and in how we can help people gain mastery over them.

We are all familiar with impulses—they are the instincts in action, they are powerful, and they come in two kinds: libidinal and aggressive, and in varying combinations of both. The Recent Shift in Attitudes toward “Acting Out”

Suzanne Bowman MSW

Suzanne Bowman

99 Lorimer Ave.
Providence, RI, 02906

Suzanne Bowman   In private practice in Providence, RI, and is a candidate-in-training at the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She is on the Board of Directors of the Rhode Island Association for the Advancement of Modern Psychoanalysis and edits its newsletter, Free Association. She is conference co-ordinator for the New England Society for Modern Group Studies and is a member of the Society of Modern Psychoanalysts.

The title of this paper refers specifically to changing attitudes toward the term “acting out,” as used in the psychoanalytic journal literature in the last decade. I ask and explore how the term “acting out” are used by psychoanalysts in the 1980s and early 1990s. What does it mean in the context of psychoanalytic treatment? Is it used differently by different schools of thought? What did it mean for analysts to prohibit patients from acting out? Does the analyst's stance of neutrality prevent acting out? Or could it actually encourage it? When is the analyst acting out in response to patient's acting-out behavior? And how does the use of this term, or lack thereof, reflect thinking about what kinds of patients can be treated in analysis? How does its use reflect the thinking about treatment?

This volume, a festchrift in honor of Robert Wallerstein, consists of an introduction by the editors, fourteen essays by Wallerstein's colleagues and associates, along with a bibliography of his scientific writings. Essays include topics that reflect areas of particular interest to Wallerstein and were chosen in consultation with him. Despite doubts and questions posed by some of the contributors, the central premise of this collection is that change as a result of psychotherapy involves alteration of psychological meaning structures. The editors phrase the question as: “How does structure, not as anatomy but as retained knowledge and meaning, change during an analytic process?” This central hermeneutic model precludes an uncritical reading by modern analysts. Although the writers are not focussed on unconscious motives for behavior, their clinical and research experience, attention to drive derivatives and choice of case studies contribute to a serious consideration of their articles.

In the opening essay, “Personality structure and the process of change, “Horowitz provides a series of diagrams to illustrate his conceptual framework for observing therapeutic change. Schematically minded readers will find this helpful. We would agree that change occurs in the modifications of processes demonstrated in the transference. We differ with Horowitz in his belief that inhibitions and fears which arise from the unconscious can be overridden solely by conscious efforts once they are brought into the transference.

Lucy Johnson

Lucy Johnson

Lucy Johnson  

Nicolosi treats male homosexuals who want to give up their homosexuality. He takes the unequivocal position that homosexuality is neither genetic nor simply an alternative lifestyle. He describes the American Psychiatric Association's decision in 1973 to omit homosexuality as a diagnostic category as a “politicization of psychiatry.” He asserts that Gay Affirmative Therapy encourages homosexuals to identify with their pathology and call it health, and that his clients have been “victims” of this kind of thinking.

Reparative therapy, which borrows heavily from psychoanalytic theory about the preoedipal origins of homosexuality, particularly the work of Charles Socarides, sees homosexuality as a developmental deficit. Most homosexuals, according to Nicolosi, fail to successfully complete the gender identity phase, in that they are unable to individuate from their mothers and develop a masculine identification through their fathers. Intrusive, anxious mothers and neglectful, emotionally unavailable fathers create an environment which makes it impossible for the prehomosexual boy to claim his maleness. Early homosexual sex play is often an attempt to secure masculinity through contact with other males. The masculine deficit is projected onto idealized males. What cannot be identified with, is eroticized. Other males are either overvalued or denigrated with a defensive detachment.

Though Nicolosi's theories are clearly influenced by psychoanalysis, his clinical technique diverges from both classical and modern analysis. He insists that homosexuals can't work with the neutral analyst. They need a “benevolent provocateur” to become a salient male presence, a father, a mentor, a teacher.

This collection of essays concerns the history and potential application of psychoanalytic thinking to the interpretation of visual art. The author, and art historian as well as practicing analyst, discusses primarily European painting and sculpture—Renaissance through Modern art. Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Caravaggio, Artemisia

115

Gentileschi, Rembrandt, Henry Moore, Brancusi, and Picasso receive special attention.

Professor Adams takes her theoretical orientation primarily from the formulations of classical analysis, beginning with a discussion of controversies aroused by Freud's study of Leonardo. In chapters on “Art and the Oedipus complex,” “Dreams, delusions, and art,” and “Psychoanalytic readings of primal scene iconography,” selected works of art serve to illustrate and exemplify particular themes in psychoanalytic theory. In addition to Freud, Winnicott's conception of the transitional object and Lacan's ideas about the riverting power of the “gaze” are introduced and used for purposes of interpretation.

The author enumerates four main categories of psychoanalytic interpretation as applied to visual art: symbolism, sublimation, creativity, and psychobiography. The first of these is equivalent to iconography in the sense of the assignment of meanings to images or their elements. The annuciation in Christian art, for example, has been identified by psychoanalytic thinkers as a primal scene image in which the Virgin Mary is impregnated by God. Ernest Jones published a paper to this effect entitled “The Madonna's conception through the ear.” Adams traces visual metaphors of impregnation in works by Van Eyck, Piero della Francesca, and Titian. The power of these images, she claims, is their fulfillment of unconscious incestuous impulses on the part of the beholder.

Professor Adams recognizes sublimation as one of the most elusive concepts in classical analysis, pointing out that Freud never arrived at a satisfactory theoretical formulation of it. In her chapter on psychobiography, the author takes this idea to mean the transformation into art of the wish to commit “the two oedipal crimes of the unconscious, incest and murder” (p. 291). Her chapters on psychobiography, that is, using details of an artist's childhood, memories, dreams, and the course of his or her life to illuminate the form and content of his work, are the most satisfying parts of the book. There are provocative discussions of the life and work of Caravaggio, Artemisia Gentileschi, Henry Moore, and the famous libel trial between the critic John Ruskin and the painter James Whistler.

This book is a welcome addition to the sparse literature on an important and all-too-often neglected population: the elderly. It serves as a practical guide for the professional and layperson alike in that it covers areas of interest and concern to both. The first part, by Claire M. Brody, deals with nursing homes; the second, prepared by Joy C. Rich and Paula Kaminsky-Davis, covers “Community Programs for the Elderly”; the third, of greatest interest to clinicians, is “Private Practice” by Vicki G. Semel; the fourth and last is devoted to Medicare.

The chapters written by Vicki G. Semel offer the best insight into how modern psychoanalytic techniques are used to great advantage in working with the elderly. The cases presented demonstrate that those techniques are as effective with older patients as they are for all other categories of patients.

Also useful for the impaired elderly population are other non-psychoanalytic treatment modalities such as “Reminiscence Groups.” Although they require very active participation by the leader, they can have very beneficial effects in bringing about socialization for those who might tend to become alienated from a social setting.

This informative collection of papers from the 21st Annual Margaret Mahler Symposium on Child Development focuses on the analytic psychotherapy of incest. The papers present a valuable perspective on the etiology and treatment of these difficult cases from a psychoanalytic point of view informed by the object relations theory of Mahler. Detailed and moving clinical illustrations underscore psychodynamic configurations which suggested to these practitioners that incest had occurred in their patients' pasts. The authors demonstrate how this knowledge framed their understanding of the transference/countertransference matrix in each case.

The book's uniqueness resides in the unusual combination of clinical cases provided by seven psychoanalysts, and related theoretical and technical discussions which demonstrate an understanding of the intrapsychic world of incest victims and their families.

This book is recommended to therapists and students who want to expand their capacity for identifying, understanding and treating victims of incest.

Acts of self-mutilation, and specifically cutting, have always been treated as suicide acts, gestures, or cries for help. Aggressive wishes may motivate impulsivity and inhibition. Since destructive impulsivity seems most likely to occur when the patient has no commitments to anyone, modern psychoanalysts focus first on fostering a narcissistic transference within which a patient may discharge tension in the presence of another person. When the repetition compulsion enters the transference, the patient is driven to repeat negative emotional experiences with the analyst. [[RunningHead]]

Notes on Narcissistic Resistance

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

What is Resistance?

Without resistance there can be no analysis (Freud, 1914; Jones, 1953). Resistance may be defined as a “counterforce in the patient, operating against the progress of the analysis” (Greenson, 1967, p. 60). These statements are both true, yet they appear to be mutually contradictory. How can an essential element in the analytic process also present an obstacle to it? To account for this seeming paradox, one must first understand the origin and nature of resistance and what role it plays in analysis.*

One approach to this question is to consider what the analytic process would be “ideally,” in the absence of resistance. We know that the answers to all of the patient's problems lie within him. When resistance is resolved, we observe that repressions are lifted and submerged material rises to the surface. Were the patient free of resistance and able to unburden himself without restrictions, the total process of his psychic development would be revealed. All the events of his life with their appropriate affect, all the conflicts associated with them, all the distortions in psychic development that proceeded from them, and all the protean transference attitudes, would pass in review, and the healing process would take care of itself.

Regrettably, this utopian ideal is unattainable.

*The discussion that follows deals with the patient's resistance. For discussion of the analyst's countertransference resistance, see Epstein and Feiner (1979), Margolis (1978), Spotnitz (1979). The two forms of resistance are interrelated and may each evoke the other. See Grotstein (1981) and Ogden (1982) for the projective identificatory process involved.*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 9, No. 2, 1984.179

[[RunningHead]]

Research in Modern Psychoanalysis

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

This article attempts to spell out the steps to be taken and the areas in which to take them, by way of supplementing the modern analytic research principles set forth by Meadow (1981, 1984) in earlier issues of this journal. Freud (1987) has described scientific creativity as “the succession of daringly playful fantasy and relentlessly realistic critisism” (p. 83)—in other words, an interplay of primary and secondary process. Under these conditions, rationality is intermittently suspended, ego boundaries are similarly rendered permeable, while the final esthetic derives from the merging of form and substance. In the psychoanalytic context, scientific creativity is fueled by curiosity about psychic process, and in the best of worlds the aim is to attain a state of illumination which goes by the name of meaning. In more mundane clinical circumstances, the artist strives to be something of a scientist, and the scientist something of an artist, the two joining hands to guide the healer toward his incremental therapeutic successes.

If we apply this line of thought to the actualities of clinical psychoanalysis, we find ourselves caught up in a web crosshatched of received wisdom and open-ended potentialities. And who is to say where the one ends and the other begins?

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 14, No. 2, 1990.241

[[RunningHead]]

The Object-Oriented Question: A Contribution to Treatment Technique

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

Introductory Observations

The object-oriented question is a technical device favored in the treatment of the preoedipal patient (Spotnitz, 1969, 1976). It is, to all appearances, relatively uncomplicated, and seems to play a largely protective role in safeguarding the patient's fragile ego from experiencing more tension that it can tolerate. If, in the process, it helps resolve resistance and fosters the development of the narcissistic transferences, these appear at first glance to be serendipitous spinoffs of the analyst's ego-sheltering approach. It is the purpose of this paper, however, to demonstrate the contrary, namely, that the object-oriented question occupies a central position and exerts an influence disproportionate to its apparent simplicity on every aspect of the treatment process.

What is an object-oriented question? It is a question calculated to direct the patient's attention away from his own ego and toward objects or events external to himself. What is the man's name? What was the movie about? Would I behave like that? The analyst asks this type of question because of the emotional state of the narcissistic patient. The latter is arrested in the narcissistic phase of development where self and object are not as yet completely separated and the one is often confused with the other. The ego of such a person is unstable, shifting in outline, unsure of its functions, and insecure in relation to the external world.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 8, No. 1, 1983.187

Anaclitic countertransference refers to feelings arising in the analyst over the course of treatment which are best understood as feelings patients needed but never received from their early objects. Eugene Goldwater MD

Eugene Goldwater   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who practices in Holyoke and Brookline, MA. He is a faculty member at the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies.

Non-impulsive people live in a world of both space and time. They experience a past, a present, and a future. Impulsive people, at least to the extent that they are impulsive, live only in the present. Non-impulsive people use fantasy to help control both their present and their future. Impulsive people use fantasy to help control both their present and their future. Impulsive pepole are deficient in this ability. In addition, because constructive actions take more time than destructive ones, impulsive people have an inherent tendency to be aggressive, thereby eliciting aggressive responses from their environment. Impulsive people do have fantasies, but they are spatial and superficial, like cartoons. They are narcissistic, and therefore unrealistic. In children, the development of the ability to use fantasy constructively involves the anticipation of reliable gratifications, and other positive experiences with fantasy. The same considerations apply to impulsive patients in a maturational form of treatment. Their therapy needs to be a pleasurable and educational experience.

Phyllis Meadow   Founder and Chair of the Board of Trustees of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the Executive Director of the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She is the editor of this journal, and founder and former President of the Society of Modern Psychoanalysts. She has served on the Board of Directors of the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis as Membership Director and was a founder of NAAP. She has authored numerous papers. She practices in New York City and Boston.

Speaking as an impulsive person, I will object to some of Goldwater's statements about us, but I would also like to tell you how creative and impulsive I find his thinking. I don't know many people who will agree with my ideas but that's probably because not many impulsives have the time to write. Impulsive people are oriented in space, not time, Goldwater tells us, and when they have fantasies they are unrealistic and based on immediate needs and the environment. Since impulsives do not live in time, they cannot have fantasies about the past or the future. They do not use fantasies as substitutes for their impulses, nor do they use them to plan what they do and do not want to do in the future. Because they live without planning, their actions will tend to be destructive.

I think this view, proposed by Goldwater, may be a phenomenological view of impulsiveness that provides us with a clear clinical description of the subject, but I would like to add another perspective. I do agree with Goldwater when he says that impulses arise from stress or need, and when acted upon they relieve the stress or need in the short term. While tension reduction and partial discharge of unacceptable impulses may be a correct explanation of impulsiveness, it may be an insufficient explanation. For a fuller explanation, I would suggest we define the observed impulsiveness in terms of internal mental events.

Narcissistic Transference: Further Considerations

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

In an earlier paper (Margolis, 1979), the writer offered some preliminary observations on the origins, development and implications for therapy of the narcissistic transference. The present article explores additional aspects of the concept, with the aim of establishing more fully its theoretical and clinical scope.

What is Narcissistic Transference?

Briefly, narcissistic transference is a special form of transference established by the narcissistic patient in the course of analytic therapy. Its characteristics are determined by such factors as the stage of early development at which the patient is arrested, the level of ego formation associated with that stage, and the nature of the experiences that the patient underwent at the time. The narcissistic patient is arrested at some point or points in approximately the first two years of life. In Mahler's (1968, 1975) widely accepted schema of psychological growth, this crucial period covers the first thirty months of life and embraces the developmental stages of normal autism, symbiosis and separation-individuation. Ego formation is conceived as proceeding from one stage to the next. Normal autism is an undifferentiated, objectless state. In the symbiotic period, self and object begin to appear, investing an emergent ego with their ambiguously differentiated images.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 6, No. 2, 1978.149

Introductory Remarks

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall  

Welcome to an exposition of mainstream modern psychoanalysis! For readers familiar with the ways and byways of modern psychoanalysis, Margolis provides a coherent, stimulating, and satifying review. For experienced psychoanalysts with no modern psychoanalytic training, Margolis presents a clear, balanced, and comprehensive rendition of the basic theory, techniques, and process of modern psychoanalysis. For the aspiring analyst, Margolis offers a vivid, emotional, and comfortable voyage into the essential modern psychoanalysis. For the aspiring analyst, Margolis offers a vivid, emotional, and comfortable voyage into the essential modern psychoanalytic realm.

Margolis's written work falls into four clearly discernible groups: Clinical concept—transference (1979, 1981), countertransference (1978), and resistance (1984); Clinical techniques—object-oriented questions (1983), contact functioning (1983), and mirroring /joining (1986); Overview (1987), Research (1990)

The orderly unfolding of Margolis's ideas is apparent not only in the above sequence, but is present in each of this papers. His writing style flows rhythmically, allowing for easy reading and comprehension of complex psychological ideas. The papers are well balanced in terms of theory, useful techniques and illustrative clinical vignettes. Using Spotnitz's work as a touchstone, Margolis leads the reader in a gentle yet scholarly manner through modern psychoanalytic labyrinths. Using no idle worlds or obscure sentences, he sparks one's imagination about significant aclinical issues. he not only comprehends modern psychoanalysis, but eloquently amplifies, clarifies, and integrates major terms and techniques.

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

A Bridge to the Object

The ego has been described as a substructure of personality defined by its functions (Hartmann, 1950). Among these, Freud (1933) especially emphasized the importance of the functions that are directed toward reality, i.e., toward objects, representing the urge toward need- and wish-fulfillment. A conceptualization of this aspect of ego development has emerged in recent years in the writings of Hyman Spotnitz and his co-workers (Spotnitz, 1961, 1963a, 1963b, 1967, 1968, 1969, 1976; Spotnitz & Meadow, 1976; Spotnitz & Nagelberg, 1952; Spotnitz, Nagelberg, & Feldman, 1953, 1956; Borowitz, 1978). Out of their experiences in treating narcissistic patients, they have identified a contact function of the ego which reflects the person's capacity to perceive an other, to reach out to him, and to establish a relationship with him as object. As Spotnitz (1963a) defines it, the contact function represents “the patient's … direct attempts to elicit some personal information about the analyst or to involve the analyst in some emotional problem he is unable to express in words” (p. 54).

The term “contact” in the context of psychic development was introduced by Winnicott in 1945, when he stated that “at the start a simple contact with external or shared reality has to be made [by the infant]” (p. 154).

Joining, Mirroring, Psychological Reflection: Terminology, Definitions, Theoretical Considerations

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

Joining is a powerful technique for resolving narcissistic resistance in psychoanalytic therapy. Its very power, however, calls for prudence in determining when and how to apply it. In the hands of the uninitiated, and used without reference to the larger maturational purpose which it aims to advance, joining, especially in its dystonic form, may subserve analytic aggrandizement against the patient; at worst, it may destroy the analysis. In this spirit, Spotnitz (1976) warns against using the joining technique as “a gimmick, a device that can be flicked on mechanically” (p. 42), and Nelson and Nelson (1957) similarly advise against “shotgun” application (p. 12).

The nucleus of therapy with the preoedipal patient is in the transference-countertransference relationship, reflected in the patient's evolving feelings toward the analyst and the latter's perception of the process through the medium of his own induced feelings. Generally speaking, technical skills such as joining come into perspective only as they further the objectives of a comprehensive therapeutic design associated with the patient-analyst relationship. The joining technique, powerful as it is, has no intrinsic significance. It is means to an end. Its value derives wholly from its role as handmaiden of a clinical method. If, therefore, we elect to study its many uses in treatment and to trace the sources of its effectiveness, we do so only in order to clarify how modern analysis goes about its pursuit of larger analytic goals.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 11, No. 1 & 2, 1983.211

Narcissistic Transference: The Product of Overlapping Self and Object Fields

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

The Concept

Freud (1905) regarded transference as one of the two pillars of psychoanalysis, the other being resistance. In his metaphor, transferences are “new editions or facsimiles” of old emotional experiences, and “they replace some earlier person by the person of the physician.” In a similar vein, Greenson (1967) defines transference as “the experience of feelings to a person which do not befit that person and which actually apply to another. Essentially, a person in the present is reacted to as though he were a person in the past.” Until recent times in clinical theory, “the past” was understood to refer to the patient's oedipal period and the “earlier person” to a significant object of that period whose characteristics the patient now attributes to the analyst.

The ego of the oedipal child is relatively advanced in terms of function and identity. Self and object, child and parent, are perceived by the child as separate entities. When this situation is later replicated in the transference, the patient who is arrested at the oedipal period sees the analyst as a clearly delineated object who represents an earlier well-defined parental figure, both differentiated from the patient's self, past and present. Thus, for example, when such a patient accuses the analyst of being sly and deceptive, he is displacing onto him his impression of an imago of his one-time oedipal period.

The narcissistic patient differs form this picture.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 4, No. 2, 1983.139

In this clearly written, well-documented presentation, Giovacchini discusses patients with severe characterological problems and primitive mental states as well as those categorized as having borderline psychopathology. He feels that since there is no consensus as to the clinical characteristics of the borderline patinet, rigid definitions are inappropriate. He prefers to think of a borderline spectrum which he identifies from three frames of reference: phenomenological observations, developmental levels, and structural defects. He expresses the need to emphasize and study intrapsychic factors rather than symptomatology. He believes that the stress on biological concepts and pharmacological treatement tends to minimize intrapsychic factors and claims that the aim of such treatment is symptom relief, not the integrity of the patient as an autonomous and worthwhile person. His goal is to convert the borderline patient into a sensitive introspective human instead of a constricted person. He demonstrates his methods for doing this with numerous detailed clinical examples.

He describes patients in the borderline spectrum as being concrete and mechanistic in their thinking. Many can move into a psychotic state and can reintegrate.

Vicki Semel

Vicki Semel

Vicki Semel  

This book consists of a collection of papers written between 1954 and 1991 covering the three areas of the English psychoanalyst Enid Balint's professional development: as psychoanalyst in the “consulting room”; as consultant and group leader to general medical practitioners; and as supervisor to marital therapists. She is associated with the independent tradition of British psychoanalysis and frequently quotes Freud, Ferenczi, Bion and Winnicott, as well as her husband Michael Balint. “Afterthoughts,” an interview with Juliet Mitchell, is offered as a dialogue between the two psychoanalysts.

Balint demonstrates how a clinician operates when she listens to the patient, developing technique and theory only after an understanding develops. Her struggle to hear the preoedipal patient is evident even though her training had emphasized the oedipal nature of neuroses. She describes, in detailed clinical case presentations, how she tried increasignly to behave as as a nonintrusive presence for patients with preverbal disorders. She learned to follow the patient's lead and developed her theoretical concepts only after a detailed examination of the case.

The articles also reveal a shift in her assumptions about the patient's alleged awareness of a distinct object. Her later articles on treatment accept a quite distinct underlying assumption. “It is only relatively recently that I stopped assuming there was more than one person in the room, and that there was a relationship even if the patient did not think so” (p. 232).

Balint is able to work with this disconcerting state through the “mirror image.” “I see him as relating to himself in the mirror, and finding someone else; and then not being able to, and then being able to again. I think, but I am not sure about this, that gradually I am being seen in the mirror when he looks at himslef. There is the looker, and there is what is in the mirror” (p. 233). Balint believes that the ability to create the perception of another is an “imaginative creation” or “imaginative perception” that can grow from analysis and enable people to be aware of others.

Narcissistic Countertransference: Emotional Availability and Case Management

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

History

Countertransference is a phenomenon whose existence was recognized very early in the history of psychoanalysis. Freud (1910, 1915) gave the term to the unconscious reactions of the analyst to his patient, resulting from the analyst's own unresolved unconscious conflicts. He considered it an unwelcome intrusion which interfered with the objective conduct of the analysis, and he recommended that the analyst make efforts to overcome it. With some exceptions, this view prevailed in analytic circles until fairly recently. Beginning in the 1950's, however, modifications of this attitude began to appear as some early investigators (A. Reich, 1951; Gitelson, 1952) noted the importance of countertransference in the analytic process. This trend became more pronounced with the development of ego psychology and object relations theory and their applications in the treatment of schizophrenia and the borderline disorders in general (Fromm-Reichman, 1952; Rosenfeld, 1952; Searles, 1967). At the present time, it is safe to say that countertransference has come to be recognized as a significant component in the therapy of narcissistic disorders.

Kernberg (1975), reviewing the literature, finds two contrasting approaches to the concept, the classical and the totalistic. The former adheres essentially to Freud's views. The latter sees countertransference as “the total emotional reaction of analyst to patient” (p. 49), including the patient's and the analyst's reality needs.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 3, No. 2, 1978.161

Treatment and Transition: Observations on Modern Psychoanalysis

B. Margolis PHD

B. Margolis

B. Margolis   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder, training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis; and an adjunct professor at the Union for Experimenting Colleges and Universities. He is also the author of many papers on modern psychoanalytic technique.

The modern analytic approach to therapy is determined by the narcissistic patient's universe which it addresses. The narcissistic patient brings to therapy problems rooted in events of the earliest days of life, a period that is ruled by programmed maturational processes. Good mothering permits these processes to unfold successfully. Defective mothering thwarts them and results in maturational lags and uneven ego formation. In both cases, the relationship between mother and child in this preverbal period is based on emotional communication and non-verbal cues. To succeed, the psychotherapy of the narcissistic patient must likewise emphasize the affective dimension of the patient-analyst interchanges, taking as its model the mother-infant relationship. This is the modern analytic approach.

Winnicott

Of all classical analytic writers, Winnicott (1965) provides the closest approximation of the therapeutic framework within which modern psychoanalysis operates. Speaking of the mother's “primary maternal preoccupation,” he states: “In my view this is the thing that gives the mother her special ability to do the right thing. She knows what the baby could be feeling like. No one else knows. … My thesis is that what we do in therapy is to attempt to imitate the natural process that characterizes the behavior of any mother of her own infant.

*This article originally appeared in Modern Psychoanalysis, Vol 12, No. 2, 1987.227
